extracted.intended_audience: educated general public and higher-education instructors/administrators (readers of Popular Science Monthly)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and normative statements about how science should be taught in secondary and university education — what faculties to develop, how to set examinations, and what kinds of problems are appropriate. Also recommendations on selecting regions of geographic/scientific exploration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overemphasis on the computative faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: The teaching of science has tended to give an impulse to the computative, to the disadvantage of the judicial and appreciative functions of students' minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science teaching should not reduce intellectual training to numerical/computative exercises alone; it must also cultivate judgment, appreciation, and decision-making needed for many branches of life-work (artistic, literary, law, medicine, business).

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop imaginative and judgment faculties alongside computation
rubrics_metrics.description: Men in after-life are called upon to use their imaginative powers, to sift evidence, and to weigh symptoms, as well as to solve problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curricula and instruction should provide tasks and experiences that exercise imagination and the faculty of judgment, not only demonstrations or algebraic manipulations. Balance numerical practice with activities that require interpretation, evidence-sifting, and decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use problem-solving as a test in experimental sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: It is now universally admitted that numerical exercises are necessary in the study of the experimental sciences, both as giving practice in the application of the various theories, and as affording tests of ability to comprehend as well as to apply that which has been learned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical and applied problems are appropriate and necessary for testing thorough knowledge in experimental sciences; they train application of theory and comprehension. However, problems must be well-designed (see related criteria) to truly test ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure examination problems are fair tests, not riddles
rubrics_metrics.description: The problems themselves are often open to comment, as partaking of the nature of enigmas, or riddles, rather than as fair tests of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid contrived or puzzle-like questions that fascinate examiners but fail to be a fair measure of a candidate's knowledge. Do not set questions that lead to indeterminate equations or infinite families of solutions when asking for demonstrable physical reasoning; such questions belong to algebra, not physics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design matriculation/entry examinations to balance openness and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary and initial step of the whole university career; a gate to further knowledge, which should be prudently left as wide open as is consistent with a reasonably high standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entry exams should not be unduly exclusionary by requiring excessive or inappropriate difficulty of young candidates. Keep the gate sufficiently open to admit diverse talents while maintaining appropriate academic standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match examination content to the subject's proper domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances cited where a question in a physics paper involved an indeterminate equation, of which the solutions were infinite in number — 'Surely this should have been relegated to its kindred algebra.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that questions test the conceptual and practical aspects of the stated discipline. Do not conflate algebraic puzzles with physics problems; align problems with disciplinary aims and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine numerical analysis with imaginative and constructive faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: The combination of the highest powers of numerical analysis with the imaginative, constructive, and inventive faculty is desirable (exemplified by men like Stokes, Thomson, Clerk-Maxwell, and Lord Rayleigh).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor pedagogies and appointments that nurture both rigorous quantitative skill and creative/inventive thinking; cultivate teachers who embody both traits to guide students effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject curriculum reforms to critique and improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: That all, or most, of [the old classical curriculum] has been swept away is ground for un- mixed satisfaction. But it does not absolutely follow that what is being substituted for it is beyond comment or improvement. There may be errors and pedantries developing in the new as in the older system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat curriculum changes as provisional and open to constructive criticism. Continuously evaluate new pedagogical practices for emerging pedantries or errors and adjust accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select exploration targets for scientific richness and map-deficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Point out regions of Europe and Asia which have not yet been explored — areas with inexact maps or defective geography, coasts and river beds only superficially known, and tracts (e.g., basins of Khatanga and Anabara, regions east of the Lena, interior of Kamchatka) promising geological, botanical, zoological, or ethnological discoveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize exploration of areas with: (a) imperfect or hypothetical cartography; (b) unique geological features (active volcanoes, mineral wealth); (c) rich or unrecorded flora and fauna; (d) ethnographic/linguistic interest (heterogeneous or aboriginal populations); (e) potential economic importance (coal, minerals, river sources). Provide accurate surveys and interdisciplinary teams (geologist, botanist, zoologist, ethnologist) for fullest scientific return.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match explorer expertise to research goals (anthropology/linguistics needs)
rubrics_metrics.description: To make anthropological and linguistic researches successful, one must of course be an accomplished scholar in Oriental linguistics and philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning ethnological or linguistic fieldwork, ensure team includes specialists trained in local languages and relevant humanistic disciplines; complex anthropological questions require scholarly linguistic competence and cultural knowledge.
